Rule: What stays in the inbox, and only this. (1) Open asks: the mail asks you to do something that matters (pay, sign, verify, fix, decide, reply, show up) and it is not done; failed, declined or overdue payments; a bill that will not pay itself; possible fraud or a security problem you did not cause; an open alert about a production system you run. It stays until a later email shows it is done, until its deadline if it names one, or until 14 days pass with no follow-up. (2) People waiting for you: a real person wrote, the newest message is theirs, and it asks you something or needs an answer (up to 14 days), or you have not opened it yet (up to 7 days). (3) What you need for something in the next 14 days: an event, appointment, trip, pickup, office visit or first day, and the confirmation, code or instructions to bring or follow; until the date has passed. (4) An unopened personal message from your doctor or care team, up to 14 days. (5) Mail you starred. Not kept, even inside a process you are in (a job change, a move, a car sale or purchase, a tax return) and even if unread: confirmations of finished steps, one-time codes, sign-in links, passwords, sign-in alerts you caused, welcome and how-to mail with no open step, status updates that ask nothing, offers and quotes after 7 days, optional asks, and a person's message that only closes the loop (thanks, congratulations, an answer to your question) once you have opened it.
Why: The one definition of what stays. Everything else is archived by a rule below and listed once in the recap. Proposed KEEP rules apply even before you approve them, because they only protect mail.

Label: Auto/Calendar
Rule: Past events: invitations, updates, cancellations, reminders and confirmations for anything that has already happened.
Why: Calendar mail is only useful until the event.

Label: Auto/Promo
Rule: Marketing, newsletters, digests, promotions, product news and social-network notifications.
Why: Bulk mail. The Unsubscribe tab lists every sender so you can stop it at the source.

Label: Auto/Receipts
Rule: Receipts, order confirmations, payment confirmations, payouts, interest and refund notices. Gmail's Purchases tab is not proof: a fee warning or a support ticket is not a receipt.
Why: Records, not tasks. They stay searchable under the label.

Label: Auto/Bills
Rule: Statement-ready, bill-ready, autopay and rent-processing notices, unless the payment failed or is overdue, or autopay is not set up for that account (then R1 keeps it).
Why: A bill that pays itself needs nothing from you. One that will not pay itself stays under R1.

Label: Auto/Shipping
Rule: Shipping, delivery, return and pickup-locker updates.
Why: Tracking mail. A pickup you must go to in the next 14 days stays under R1.

Label: Auto/Security
Rule: Sign-in alerts, verification codes and security notices that you triggered yourself, once 12 hours old. This includes copies sent to you as the recovery address of another account and 'you allowed an app access' notices, when the activity matches something you did.
Why: Codes and alerts you caused are noise after a few hours. Anything you did not cause stays under R1.

Label: Auto/Alerts
Rule: Monitoring and service alerts that are resolved; open alerts about a development or test environment; and any other alert or warning (usage, quota, package update, key or certificate due) that is not about production.
Why: Open production alerts stay under R1. Name your production systems in R1 if the routine cannot tell.

Label: Auto/Notices
Rule: Informational account, service, app, banking, health, insurance, building and HR-portal notices (policy or price changes, welcome mail, plan updates, usage reports, credits, explanations of benefits, reminders for dates that passed) with nothing for you to do.
Why: The largest kind of automated mail. Anything with an open ask stays under R1.

Label: Auto/Notices
Rule: Finished and superseded asks: an automated request, reminder, problem notice or one-time code for a step that a later email shows is done (the check is complete, the payment went through, the document was signed); and when a newer email from the same sender repeats the same ask or notice, or the same message sits in the inbox twice, the older copies (keep the one you replied to or forwarded, otherwise the newest).
Why: Without this, three reminders hold one task, and a paid bill keeps its failed-payment notice. The later email is the proof, and the reason column names it.

Label: Auto/Notices
Rule: Optional asks: an automated invitation to do something you do not have to do (vote your shares, enroll in an add-on or protection plan, take a survey), even when it names a deadline. Not covered: anything that costs you money, access or a penalty if you ignore it (R1 keeps those), and asks from a person.
Why: These name a deadline, so they look urgent, but nothing happens if you ignore them.

Label: Auto/Notices
Rule: Older recap emails from this routine: keep only the newest one.
Why: So recaps do not pile up.

Label: Auto/Done
Rule: Finished conversations: you sent the newest message and nothing has arrived since, or the other side's last message only closes the loop (thanks, congratulations, an answer to your question) and you have opened it. Support tickets and marketplace conversations whose order, trip or request is over.
Why: If they write again, Gmail brings the thread back to the inbox.

Label: Auto/Recruiting
Rule: Recruiter, sourcer and hiring outreach about roles you are not pursuing (cold messages, follow-ups and their replies), at any age, answered or not. Not covered: a hiring process you are actively in (interviews scheduled, an offer, onboarding); R1 keeps what needs you there.
Why: Turn this off while you are job hunting.

Label: Auto/Junk
Rule: Likely phishing or junk that got past the spam filter: an unsolicited email from a sender you have never written to that poses as a document, e-signature, invoice, delivery or account notice, where the sender's address does not belong to the service it imitates and it ties to nothing you are doing.
Why: The routine never deletes mail or marks it as spam. Junk is archived and listed with a warning in the recap.

Label: Auto/Aged
Rule: Catch-all: everything else goes after one recap. Any thread that no KEEP rule keeps and no other rule names is archived at the first run after it arrives, whatever its age and whether or not you opened it. The recap lists each one with its reason and flags anything about money, a deadline or security.
Why: This is what keeps the inbox short: the default is to archive, and only KEEP rules keep. It is always checked last, wherever it sits in the sheet, and mail it keeps taking turns into proposals for specific rules. Turn it off to run the other way round: mail no rule names stays in the inbox and gets a rule proposal instead.
